header.subject: English
header.centralFocus: Narrative Writing: Dialogue and Inner Thoughts

A: RL.9-10.3: Analyze how complex characters develop over the course of a text, interact with other characters, and advance the plot or develop the theme.
W.9-10.3.b: Use narrative techniques, such as dialogue, pacing, description, reflection, and multiple plot lines, to develop experiences, events, and/or characters.

RL.9-10.5: Analyze how an author’s choices concerning how to structure a text, order events within it (e.g., parallel plots), and manipulate time (e.g., pacing, flashbacks) create such effects as mystery, tension, or surprise.
B: Students have read Six of Crows up to chapters 19 and 20. Chapters 19 and 20 was the most recent reading assignment, and the chapters are dialogue-heavy between Nina and Matthias. In these chapters, the background on their “forbidden love” is revealed.
Students will use their understanding of the story and their own life experiences. Specifically, how they communicate with people in their lives in contrast to what they think.
C: Dialogue must serve a purpose. It must reveal something about a character, show the character’s relationship to someone or something else, reveal conflict, create tension, or move the story forward. Inner thoughts work alongside dialogue to demonstrate subtext or a character’s internal conflict.
**Inner Thought** – The characters’ or narrator’s private thoughts
**Subtext** – What the contrast between what’s being said and what’s being thought tells the reader.
D: **SWBAT:** Students will be able to analyze Bardugo’s use of dialogue and inner thoughts in chapters 19 and 20 to develop the relationship between Nina and Matthias, and apply these techniques to their own narrative writing.
**EQ:** How do writers use dialogue and inner thoughts to develop characters and their relationships?
E: The book: Six of Crows, computer, tv/projector, internet access, slide presentation, whiteboard, marker, desks, chairs, pencils, graphic organizer, exist slip
F: The class will sit in their normal seats for the class, working with partners for the guided practice portion. I will ask for two volunteers to demonstrate the distance between the characters’ thoughts and dialogue in relation to the characters’ closeness.

G.title: Initiation
paragraphs: Journal Prompt: Who are you most honest with? Who is most honest with you? Why is honesty important? Is it always important to be honest?

Discussion: Does anyone have any hot-takes? What do they say to people they’re not familiar with? What do they think? Are the answers to those questions the same, close, or very different? What do they say to people they know? What do they think? Are the answers to those questions the same, close, or very different? Why do we do that?

G.title: Academic Language Instruction
paragraphs: Slide Presentation: Define dialogue and inner thoughts. Ask: Why is it important to have both? Why is it important to have either? Explain the five purposes of dialogue. Ask for two volunteers to demonstrate Bardugo’s use of dialogue and inner thoughts.

G.title: Guided Practice
paragraphs: Partner work: Students work in pairs and use their graphic organizers to locate a specific moment in chapter 19 or 20 where dialogue or inner thoughts does one of dialogue/inner thoughts’ five purposes. Students must write down the example and write why their example is effective based on the five purposes.

G.title: Independent Practice
paragraphs: Exit slip: Students apply what they’ve learned from the mentor text to their own writing

G.title: Closure
paragraphs: Review essential question: Ask students how they used a dialogue and inner thoughts in their writing. Did the thoughts match the dialogue? Why or why not?

H: Informal: Observation and 1-1 interaction during guided practice and review of the Graphic Organizer.
Formal: The exit slip – not graded, but used to assess progress. I’ll also read their journal entries.

struggling.strategy: Provide vocabulary support, specifically for the “Grishaverse” terminology. The exit slip should also have sentence examples.

Printed copies of the slides are provided with the graphic organizer. Student is also sandwiched between two of the more advanced students who have agreed privately to help peers who may be struggling.

enrichment.evidence: Reads and writes above grade level
enrichment.strategy: Challenge them to show the emotion without ever explicitly writing the emotion.

J: Vygotsky’s “Zone of Proximal Development” and “Gradual Release” models are utilized through the transition from direct instruction to partner-work on text analysis to independent application on the exit slip.
In Bloom’s Taxonomy, this lesson hits three levels: understanding, application, and analysis.

This lesson also lends itself nicely to Piaget’s schema theory. I’ll be able to activate the student’s own experience and background knowledge because every one of them has both spoken and had thoughts: dialogue and inner thoughts.
